11. Long‑form response (health topic 1)  
Childhood undernutrition, especially during the first 1,000 days (from conception to about 2 years of age), has profound, long‑lasting effects on growth, health, and learning. Stunting (low height for age) in this period reflects chronic undernutrition and repeated infections. In the short term, children who are stunted are more likely to have delayed motor milestones (such as sitting, standing, and walking), poorer language development, and reduced attention and memory, all of which harm school readiness and early cognitive performance.  

In the long term, the effects extend into adolescence and adulthood. Stunted children tend to complete fewer years of schooling, score lower on tests of literacy and numeracy, and show reduced problem‑solving skills. Biologically, poor nutrition in early life can alter brain structure (e.g., reduced dendritic branching, smaller brain volume in some regions) and function (altered neurotransmitter systems, myelination), which are difficult to reverse later. Economically, adults who were stunted as children often have lower productivity and earnings. Prevention requires adequate maternal nutrition, exclusive breastfeeding for about six months, timely introduction of nutrient‑dense complementary foods, infection prevention (sanitation, vaccines), and nutrition education for families and communities.  

12. Long‑form response (health topic 2)  
Dietary fats and fatty acids play several key roles in human health. Total fat should generally provide less than about 30% of total daily energy, and saturated fats ideally less than 10%, because high saturated fat intake raises LDL cholesterol and increases the risk of cardiovascular disease. Trans fats from partially hydrogenated oils are particularly harmful and should be minimized. In contrast, unsaturated fats—especially omega‑3 fatty acids—are beneficial for heart and brain health.  

Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a long‑chain omega‑3 fatty acid critical for the normal development and function of the brain and retina. It accumulates rapidly in the fetal and infant brain, so maternal intake during pregnancy and lactation, and infant intake during early life, are important. Omnivores and vegetarians can obtain DHA mainly from oily fish, eggs, and fortified foods. Vegans do not consume direct animal sources of DHA; although the body can convert alpha‑linolenic acid (ALA, found in flax, chia, walnuts, and some plant oils) into DHA, this conversion is inefficient. For this reason, vegan diets often rely on microalgae‑derived DHA supplements, which provide preformed DHA and help support visual and cognitive function without using animal products. Balancing total fat intake, emphasizing unsaturated fats, limiting saturated and trans fats, and ensuring adequate omega‑3 intake (including DHA) are central to healthy dietary patterns.
